newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia rebels set date for troop release.
newsitem.headline: Colombia rebels set date for troop release.

text.p: Leftist rebel commanders said on Tuesday they would release 60 Colombian soldiers they have been holding prisoner for more than nine months.
Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) guerrillas said they would also hand over 10 marines, seized in a separate battle in January.
They said the hostages would be released in a demilitarized region of southern Colombia on June 15.

The decision, reached after talks in Caqueta province between FARC leaders and government and Catholic Church representatives, marked the beginning of the end for Latin America's longest-running hostage crisis -- largely overshadowed by the recent siege of the Japanese embassy residence in Lima.

"The FARC will hand over 60 soldiers and 10 marines to the International Committee of the Red Cross and the National Conciliation Commission on June 15 in the town of Cartagena del Chaira," said a joint communique drawn up in five hours of talks.

The soldiers were captured on Aug. 30 in neighbouring Putumayo province in an attack that heralded the start of one of the bloodiest rebel offensives in three decades of armed uprising in Colombia. The marines were taken prisoner in fighting in northwest Choco province.

The FARC held Tuesday's meeting in the jungle town of Remolinos del Caguan, which took on a symbolic importance after the army refused to pull out of the community under a partial demilitarization plan in December, arguing it was a key point on rebel-controlled drug smuggling routes.

Cartagena del Chaira, chosen for the troop release, is also a symbolic choice given that it is the largest town in the 5,000 square mile (13,000 sq km) demilitarized zone and the site of one of the largest military bases.

FARC commanders Joaquin Gomez and Fabian Ramirez invited the mothers of the soldiers and international observers to the handover and said all the prisoners would receive medical checks before being released.
"This is an agreement which is not only satisfactory but will bring a painful chapter to an end," said Augusto Ramirez, member of the National Conciliation Commission.
The soldiers, once free, are due to be taken to an army base near the provincial capital Florencia for psychological debriefing, army commander Gen. Manuel Jose Bonett said.

His earlier appeal to the press not to interview the soldiers until the army gives permission seems set to go unheeded. In a clear demonstration of who is in control, the FARC chieftains said the soldiers would give a press conference to journalists before they were shipped out of the demilitarized zone.

Once the handover is complete, several hundred FARC fighters thought to be in the zone will have another week to melt back into the jungle out of the grip of the military, which will return to the zone on June 23.
